scams.name: Nanjing Road Tea House / Bar Scam
scams.description:
Nanjing Road's pedestrian shopping strip draws millions of visitors and, alongside them, a well-organized team of English-speaking scammers who have run the teahouse operation for decades. Two people — posing as domestic tourists from Xi'an or as students practicing English — approach with warm conversation and a specific invitation: a "traditional Chinese tea ceremony nearby," framed as a cultural experience you'd miss otherwise. The walk takes ten minutes; the venue is always on a side street or above ground level.

Inside, the tea is served and tastes fine. Then the bill arrives: ¥3,000–¥10,000, split across multiple teas ordered without your awareness of the pricing. Staff position themselves near the door. Negotiating or refusing brings escalating pressure. A venue at 510 Tianjin Road has been documented in multiple reports as a longstanding location for this operation, but the scam runs from many addresses and the specific venue matters less than the approach pattern.

Any stranger who approaches you near Nanjing Road, People's Square, or the Bund within minutes of meeting and mentions "tea," "cultural experience," or "traditional ceremony" is running this scam — the pitch is identical every time. Walk past without stopping; for genuine Shanghai tea, go directly to the Huxinting Teahouse inside Yu Garden, where a posted menu has been in place since 1855 and no one recruits customers from the street — the difference between arriving at a chosen venue and following a stranger is the entire protection.
scams.avoidance: Walk past any stranger approaching near Nanjing Road with 'bu yao xie xie' Never follow a stranger to a 'nearby' tea house — the venue is always the scam Avoid 510 Tianjin Road (SMOOTH dining bar) and any similar side-street 'tea' venue For genuine tea, go to Shanghai Propaganda Poster Art Centre cafe or hotel-concierge-recommended venues If trapped, photograph the bill, pay with credit card (for chargeback leverage), then report to 12315 and your card company
scams.location: Nanjing Road East and West pedestrian shopping area, side streets off People's Square, Tianjin Road, Bund approach
scams.tldr: Pairs posing as Chinese tourists or students approach foreigners near Nanjing Road's pedestrian strip in fluent English, invite them to a "traditional tea ceremony," then deliver bills of ¥3,000–¥10,000 in a locked side-street venue with no posted prices and no way out without paying.

scams.name: Pudong (PVG) Airport Black Taxi & Meter Rigging
scams.description:
Pudong International Airport channels tens of thousands of international arrivals a day, and unofficial taxi touts have worked the terminal exit paths for years. Before you reach the official metered-taxi queue outside, men in casual clothes approach with confident English — "Taxi? Shanghai city? Four hundred yuan, cheap price" — projecting local authority and a sense that the offer is better than standing in line.

The metered fare from PVG to central Shanghai is ¥180–¥220 for the 45-kilometer, 50-minute ride. Touts quote double or triple that. Licensed taxis carry a separate risk: a 2025 documented case showed a meter tampered to run fast, producing fares far above the correct rate even in a marked vehicle. Longyang Road station — the Maglev endpoint — has higher tout density than the airport itself; travelers who take the Maglev and then try to hail a taxi at Longyang Road face the same problem in a less-controlled environment.

Metro Line 2 runs from Pudong Airport directly to Nanjing Road for ¥7 in 90 minutes — no negotiation required. If you need a taxi, install DiDi before arriving: the fare is set digitally, you board at the marked ride-share zone, and there is nothing to negotiate ; for a licensed metered taxi, say 打表 ("da biao" — "start the meter") before you get in and photograph the license plate from the rear window as your record.
scams.avoidance: Take Shanghai Metro Line 2 from PVG station: ¥7, 90 min, scam-proof Install DiDi before arrival; English interface, regulated fares, digital receipt If taking licensed taxi, say 'da biao' (打表) before boarding; screenshot DiDi fare as reference Photograph the taxi license number from the rear windscreen on entering If you take the Maglev, transfer to Metro Line 2/7 at Longyang Road, not a taxi
scams.location: Pudong International Airport (PVG) arrivals hall, official taxi queue, Longyang Road Maglev terminus, Hongqiao Airport (SHA) secondary
scams.tldr: Touts at Pudong Airport intercept travelers before the official taxi queue and quote ¥400–¥600 for a city ride whose metered fare is ¥180–¥220; licensed taxis carry a separate risk from tampered meters that more than double the legitimate fare.

scams.name: Bund & People's Square Wine / Champagne Bar Overcharge
scams.description:
The Bund promenade at sunset attracts a steady stream of solo foreign visitors, and a parallel team of English-fluent women works the crowd targeting men traveling alone. The approach is easy and friendly — local conversation, a warm recommendation, an offer to show you "the best view in Shanghai" — usually at a bar one or two floors above street level with a genuine river panorama. The ambiance, when you arrive, is real.

Seated inside, the ordering happens casually: "just one drink." A bottle of champagne arrives. There was never a posted price, and the discussion of what you were ordering was never precise. The bill is ¥6,000 to ¥20,000. The woman has disappeared. Staff and bouncers position between you and the door. Paying in cash or Alipay removes any chargeback option; credit-card chargebacks have succeeded in documented cases where the venue's own menu showed lower prices than the bill.

Any bar recommendation from a stranger met on the Bund is part of this operation — the approach is always casual and the view is always genuine. Choose your Bund sunset bar before leaving the hotel: Bar Rouge, M on the Bund, and the Waldorf Astoria's Long Bar all post English menus and accept card payment , so you arrive with a confirmed price rather than following a stranger to an unmarked upper-floor venue where the bill is a surprise.
scams.avoidance: Choose Bund-view bars yourself: M on the Bund, Bar Rouge, Hakkasan, Waldorf Long Bar, Peace Hotel Jazz Bar (all posted pricing, booking required) Walk past any stranger offering a 'local bar' invitation on the Bund Always verify a bar has posted English menu and card payment BEFORE ordering Pay with credit card for chargeback leverage; cash and Alipay are much harder to dispute If trapped, photograph the bill and inflated prices; dispute via card and report to 12315
scams.location: Bars near the Bund, Nanjing Road East/West side streets, People's Square north side, Xintiandi tourist-facing venues
scams.tldr: An English-speaking woman on the Bund steers solo foreign men to an unmarked upper-floor bar "with the best sunset view," orders champagne without explicit discussion, and disappears when the bill arrives — ¥6,000 to ¥20,000 — while bouncers block the exit.

scams.name: Shanghai Tea Ceremony Ambush at Yuyuan & The Bund
scams.description:
Yu Garden draws 10 million visitors a year and supports a milder version of the Nanjing Road teahouse operation. The opening is gentler and less aggressive: "Hello, we are students — can we practice English?" or "Excuse me, could you take a photo for us?" The conversation is warm and natural before the tea invitation appears within ten minutes, framed as a cultural afterthought rather than the main objective.

The tea house is nearby but off the main bazaar walkway — up a side staircase or down a lane without posted prices. Tea is served and tastes fine. The bill is ¥800–¥2,500 — lower than the Nanjing Road version but still ten to twenty times the cost at a legitimate Shanghai teahouse. Police historically assign responsibility to the tourist for willingly attending; the practical remedy is a credit-card chargeback citing the discrepancy between the bill and the venue's own posted menu.

Walk past anyone near Yu Garden who approaches in confident English and mentions tea, culture, or photos — the script is the same operation as Nanjing Road, lower-pressure. For authentic tea at Yu Garden, go directly to the Huxinting Teahouse in the middle of the Yu Garden pond: it has served tea at posted prices since 1855 and has never solicited customers from the street — arriving there on your own versus following a stranger is the only protection that works reliably.
scams.avoidance: Walk past any stranger at Yu Garden, Bund, or People's Square offering 'English practice' or 'photo help' For genuine tea at Yu Garden, visit Huxinting Teahouse (the pavilion in the middle of the pond, 1855) Published tea prices at Huxinting: ¥150–¥300 per person with clear menu Never follow a stranger to a 'nearby' tea house, even if they seem friendly Pay with credit card for chargeback leverage; report via 12315 and your card issuer
scams.location: Yu Garden (Yuyuan) bazaar area, the Bund promenade, People's Square south side, pedestrian shopping zones
scams.tldr: Students or "friendly locals" near Yu Garden bazaar approach tourists to "practice English" or ask for a photo, pivot to a "nearby traditional tea ceremony" within ten minutes, and present bills of ¥800–¥2,500 — ten to twenty times the price of a legitimate teahouse — in a venue with no posted prices.

scams.name: Shanghai Disneyland 'Fast Pass' & Fake Ticket Scams
scams.description:
Shanghai Disneyland's ticket structure — one-day, two-day, Premier Access tiers, VIP tours — creates enough complexity that touts exploit the confusion near the Disney Resort Metro station on Line 11 and at hotel concierge desks offering "bundled" packages. A reseller quotes ¥800 per person for Disney Premier Access fast-track entry, presented as an insider deal that skips the official app.

Genuine Disney Premier Access is sold exclusively through the official Shanghai Disneyland app and park entrance kiosks at ¥300–¥600 depending on daily demand. Third-party sellers charge one and a half to two times the legitimate rate for passes that may scan correctly — or may not. Outright fake tickets are QR codes that look valid on the reseller's screen but fail at the actual park gate; the tout is untraceable, the money is gone, and you are standing outside the park without a ticket.

Buy everything through the official Shanghai Disneyland app or shanghaidisneyresort.com before you travel — it handles tickets, Premier Access, and attraction reservations in English. Do not buy Disney tickets from hotel lobbies, Metro-station touts, or third-party resale sites: there is no way to verify a QR code until you reach the gate, and by then the seller is unreachable , so official purchase is the only option with any recourse if something goes wrong.
scams.avoidance: Book directly via Shanghai Disneyland official app or shanghaidisneyresort.com Disney Premier Access is ¥300–¥600; anything higher is a markup or scam Shanghai Metro Line 11 to Disney Resort station: ¥5–¥7, 40 min, scam-proof Pay with credit card for fraud protection; avoid cash/Alipay for chargeback reasons For hotel stays, book only Disney Resort Hotel or Toy Story Hotel via Disney's own site
scams.location: Shanghai Disneyland main entrance (Pudong), Disney Resort Metro station, third-party resale sites, hotel-concierge packages
scams.tldr: Touts near Shanghai Disneyland's Metro station sell fake QR-code tickets and overpriced "Disney Premier Access" passes at ¥800 — genuine Premier Access is sold only through the official Disney app at ¥300–¥600, and a fake ticket is only discovered when it fails at the gate with the seller already gone.

scams.name: AP Xinyang Fake Market Bait-and-Switch
scams.description:
AP Xinyang at the Science and Technology Museum metro station and Han City in Jing'an are Shanghai's best-known replica markets, selling fake luxury goods in a legal-grey zone tolerated for tourist traffic. Vendors display polished sample watches, handbags, and electronics in the front stalls. You choose a piece, negotiate hard, and reach a number that feels like a genuine win — ¥200 for an item originally quoted at ¥500. The vendor agrees, seems pleased, and offers to "wrap it for you in the back."

The item that comes back is a lower grade than the one you examined and held. Diamond testers, laser-engraving demonstrations, and authenticity cards are props used to reinforce confidence before the switch. The vendor's expression of surprise at any complaint is part of the routine, and there is no mechanism for returning the item once you leave the stall. A separate risk applies at customs: bringing counterfeit goods back to the US, UK, or EU is illegal — confiscation on arrival is routine for obvious fakes, with no reimbursement.

Hold onto the specific item you negotiated for yourself from the moment you agree on the price and do not release it for any reason. Inspect the item one final time before handing over cash — that moment before payment is the only window where refusing the switch carries any leverage ; once you leave the stall, there is no recourse at the market, and customs confiscation on arrival home is an additional loss on top of what you paid.
scams.avoidance: Start negotiations at 10–15% of first-quoted price; walk away if vendor refuses Hold the specific item yourself from inspection through payment; refuse 'wrapping in back' Understand home-country customs prohibit commercial counterfeits; personal-use amounts vary but risks are real Consider alternatives: Global Harbor, Xintiandi, IFC Mall for genuine shopping with returns If shopping anyway, budget only what you can afford to lose entirely
scams.location: AP Xinyang Fashion Market (Science & Technology Museum metro), Han City Fashion & Accessories Plaza, various 'underground fake' markets
scams.tldr: Vendors at AP Xinyang Market and Han City show high-grade replica watches or jewelry during negotiation, then deliver a lower-quality item from a back room after payment — plus customs seizure risk for bringing counterfeits home across most Western borders.

scams.name: Pudong Airport SIM Card Tout Markup
scams.description:
Pudong Airport's arrivals hall has both official carrier counters and an ecosystem of unofficial SIM touts who target arriving international travelers. A friendly man in casual dress or an unbranded booth offers a "tourist SIM — 30GB, 30 days, ¥300" before you reach the official carrier counters at the far end of arrivals. The price sounds plausible for China mobile data if you have no reference point.

China Mobile and China Unicom both operate labeled counters in PVG Terminal 2 arrivals, selling equivalent 30-day, 30GB plans for ¥100–¥150. Third-party touts charge double or triple and sometimes sell SIMs that stop working after seven days — leaving you without connectivity in the middle of your trip with no support contact. The tout network works in the same arrivals-hall ecosystem as black-taxi operators, sharing the assumption that tired international arrivals won't know the official counter location.

Walk past any arrivals booth not clearly labeled China Mobile or China Unicom and head to the official carrier counters at the far end of Terminal 2. The simplest approach is to buy a China eSIM through Airalo or Nomad before you fly — it activates before landing for US$15–$30 and skips the airport-counter step entirely , which matters most if you land late at night or in Terminal 1 where the official counters are harder to locate.
scams.avoidance: Buy an eSIM before flying: Airalo, Holafly, or Nomad sells China 5GB 30-day at US$15–US$30 At PVG, use ONLY the official China Unicom or China Mobile counter — ¥100–¥150 for 30 days/30GB Ignore any SIM booth not clearly carrier-branded For short trips (<10 days), home-carrier roaming is often competitive Keep a receipt (fapiao) from whichever carrier you choose for any warranty or support needs
scams.location: Pudong Airport arrivals hall, along airport transit paths, hotel check-in desks offering 'tourist SIM' packages
scams.tldr: Touts and unbranded booths at Pudong Airport's arrivals hall sell "tourist SIM cards" at ¥200–¥300 for plans that cost ¥100–¥150 at official China Mobile and China Unicom counters — and some stop working after seven days, leaving travelers without data mid-trip.
